# How to use this subject

Pharmaceutical Inorganic and Analytical Chemistry joins two subjects of the older B.Pharm course: pharmaceutical analysis (errors, impurities, all kinds of titration) and inorganic pharmaceutical chemistry (antacids, antiseptics, electrolytes, haematinics, radiopharmaceuticals). It is a 3-credit theory course of the new B.Pharm (NEP 2020): 45 lecture hours, 75 marks in all (30 sessional, 45 end-semester). The matching practical (BP111P) uses the same titrations and limit tests, so what you learn here also earns marks in the laboratory.

The notes follow the five units of the PCI B.Pharm Syllabus 2026 exactly; no unit is split or joined. Unit 3 (all titrations, 14 hours) is the longest; give it two or three days. The other units take one day each. For each day: read the notes, close them and write the equations and equivalence factors from memory, redo every worked example with a calculator, then answer the questions of that unit.

**End-semester paper (PCI Table XV, 3-credit course): 45 marks, 2 hours.** Confirm the exact pattern with your university.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | Multiple-choice / objective questions, all compulsory | 10 × 1 = 10 |
| II | Short answers: answer 5 of 7 | 5 × 4 = 20 |
| III | Long answers: answer 2 of 3 | 2 × 7.5 = 15 |

In this app the long answers are marked out of 8 (the app uses whole marks), so the full mock paper totals 46. The model long answers are written for 7.5 marks: about one and a half pages with the principle, equations, a table or diagram and 6–8 clear points. Short answers (4 marks) need about half a page: definition, principle or equation, 3–5 points, and an example. Very-short questions (2 marks) in the bank are for revision and for the objective section.

**Probability ratings**

- **High**: a standard topic of this syllabus that appears in most papers on the same content; prepare the full answer.
- **Medium**: asked every few years, or as part of a larger question.
- **Low**: less common; useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from the weight of each topic in the syllabus and from how often similar questions appear in pharmaceutical analysis and inorganic chemistry papers of the older PCI course. This is a new syllabus, so there are no past papers of this exact course yet; treat the ratings as guidance, not a promise.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics to prepare first |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Analysis, errors, impurities | Primary and secondary standards; types of errors and how to minimise them; accuracy vs precision; sources of impurities; limit tests for arsenic, iron, chloride, sulphate, heavy metals; modified limit tests |
| 2 Acid–base, buffers, electrolytes | Buffer action and Henderson–Hasselbalch numericals; isotonicity and its adjustment; functions of Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺; ORS composition and principle; physiological acid–base balance |
| 3 Titrations | Theory of indicators; neutralisation curves; non-aqueous solvents and perchloric acid titrant; Mohr/Volhard/modified Volhard/Fajans; metal ion indicators and masking; EDTA standardisation; iodimetry vs iodometry; cerimetry; gravimetry steps |
| 4 GI agents, antimicrobials, radiopharmaceuticals | Ideal antacid and combinations; sodium bicarbonate and aluminium hydroxide gel (preparation, assay); hydrogen peroxide and chlorinated lime (assay, volume strength, available chlorine); mechanism of antimicrobials; radioisotopes and safe handling |
| 5 Miscellaneous compounds | Expectorants (KI, NH4Cl); emetics (CuSO4); ferrous sulphate and gluconate; classification of antidotes; sodium thiosulphate in cyanide poisoning |

**The asterisk compounds.** The syllabus marks sodium chloride, calcium gluconate, sodium bicarbonate, aluminium hydroxide gel, hydrogen peroxide, chlorinated lime, ammonium chloride, copper sulphate and ferrous sulphate with an asterisk. For these, be ready to write the full preparation, assay and uses. For the other compounds, the principle of the assay and the uses are usually enough.

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Every assay answer should have: principle in one line → balanced equation → titrant and indicator → end point colour → "1 ml of … M … ≡ … g" → formula for %. Examiners give a mark for each.
2. Do not memorise equivalence factors blindly: learn to derive them (molar mass × molarity × mole ratio ÷ 1000). If you forget the number, show the derivation and you still earn most of the marks.
3. Write every reaction balanced; check charges in ionic equations (for example 2MnO4⁻ + 5H2O2 + 6H⁺).
4. Draw small diagrams: Gutzeit apparatus, titration curves, buffer action, red cells in hypo/iso/hypertonic solutions, time–distance–shielding.
5. Use comparison tables: iodimetry vs iodometry, Mohr vs Volhard vs Fajans, primary vs secondary standards, systemic vs non-systemic antacids, accuracy vs precision.
6. Numericals: write the formula, substitute with units, and box the answer (pH, g NaCl per 100 ml, molarity, %).
7. Learn these numbers cold: Kw 10⁻¹⁴; blood pH 7.35–7.45; HCO3⁻ : H2CO3 = 20 : 1; FP of blood −0.52 °C; FPD of 1% NaCl 0.576 °C; 0.9% NaCl isotonic; ORS 245 mOsm/L; 3% H2O2 ≈ 10 volume; chlorinated lime ≥ 30% available chlorine; half-lives I-131 8 d, Tc-99m 6 h, P-32 14 d, Co-60 5.3 y.
8. Do all ten MCQs; they are compulsory and quick, and the MCQ bank here covers the facts they usually test.

# Last-night revision sheet

## Unit 1: Analysis, errors, impurities

- Analysis: qualitative (identity), quantitative (assay), purity (limit tests). Techniques: titrimetric, gravimetric, instrumental (optical, electrochemical, chromatographic), physical, biological.
- M = moles/L; N = M × n; H2SO4 0.1 M = 0.2 N; ppm = µg/g. % = V × f × factor × 100 ÷ weight.
- Primary standard: pure, stable, non-hygroscopic, high equivalent weight, stoichiometric (KHP, Na2CO3, NaCl, K2Cr2O7, KIO3, As2O3, Zn). Secondary: NaOH, HCl, KMnO4, thiosulphate, I2, AgNO3, EDTA, HClO4.
- Determinate (systematic) errors → accuracy; indeterminate (random) → precision. Minimise: calibration, blank, control, independent method, replicates, standard addition.
- Significant figures: +/− keep fewest decimal places; ×/÷ keep fewest significant figures.
- Impurity sources: raw materials, manufacture (reagents, intermediates, by-products, solvents, catalysts), vessels, atmosphere, storage, cross-contamination, adulteration.
- Limit tests (Nessler cylinders, test vs standard): Cl⁻ AgNO3 + HNO3; SO4²⁻ BaCl2 reagent + HCl (K2SO4 seeds); Fe thioglycollic acid + citric acid + NH3 (purple); As Gutzeit (Zn/HCl, KI, SnCl2, lead acetate cotton, HgCl2 paper yellow); Pb dithizone red (KCN masks); heavy metals thioacetamide pH 3.5 as ppm Pb. Modified tests remove effervescence, colour or insolubility.

## Unit 2: Acid–base, buffers, isotonicity, electrolytes

- Arrhenius / Brønsted–Lowry / Lewis. pH = −log[H⁺]; weak acid pH = ½(pKa − log C).
- Buffer = weak acid + salt / weak base + salt. pH = pKa + log(salt/acid). Max capacity at pH = pKa; β = ΔB/ΔpH.
- Acetate 0.1/0.2 → pH 5.06; NH3/NH4Cl 1:1 → 9.25.
- Isotonic 0.9% NaCl, FP −0.52 °C. W = (0.52 − a)/0.576; NaCl equivalent method. Hypotonic → haemolysis; hypertonic → crenation.
- ECF: Na⁺, Cl⁻, HCO3⁻; ICF: K⁺, Mg²⁺, phosphate. Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase.
- NaCl 1 g = 17.1 mEq; KCl 1 g = 13.4 mEq; IV K⁺ always diluted, slow.
- ORS/L: NaCl 2.6, glucose 13.5, KCl 1.5, trisodium citrate 2.9 g; 245 mOsm/L; Na–glucose co-transport.
- Acid–base: buffers → lungs → kidneys; HCO3⁻ : H2CO3 20 : 1; four disorders.

## Unit 3: Titrations

| Acidimetry | 1 M HCl (Na2CO3) | Methyl orange | NaHCO3 0.08401 g |
| Back titration | 1 M HCl + 1 M NaOH | Methyl red | NH3 0.01703 g |
| Alkalimetry (formol) | 0.1 M NaOH (KHP) | Phenolphthalein | NH4Cl 0.005349 g |
| Non-aqueous | 0.1 M HClO4 in AcOH (KHP) | Crystal violet | Sodium benzoate 0.01441 g |
| Argentometry | 0.1 M AgNO3 (NaCl) | K2CrO4 / Fe³⁺ alum | NaCl 0.005844 g |
| Complexometry | 0.05 M EDTA (Zn) | EBT pH 10 | MgSO4 0.006018 g; Ca gluconate 0.02242 g (+Mg) |
| Permanganometry | 0.02 M KMnO4 (oxalic acid) | Self | H2O2 0.001701 g |
| Cerimetry | 0.1 M Ce(IV) (As2O3) | Ferroin | FeSO4·7H2O 0.02780 g |
| Iodometry | 0.1 M thiosulphate (K2Cr2O7) | Starch, late | CuSO4·5H2O 0.02497 g |
| Iodimetry | 0.05 M I2 | Starch | Na2S2O3·5H2O 0.02482 g |
| Iodate (Andrews) | 0.05 M KIO3 | CHCl3 layer | KI 0.01660 g |

- Indicator theories: Ostwald (ionisation) and quinonoid (structure). Equivalence pH: SA–SB 7, WA–SB ~8.7 (phenolphthalein), SA–WB ~5.3 (methyl orange/red). Boric acid + glycerin.
- Non-aqueous solvents: aprotic, protophilic (DMF, pyridine — for weak acids), protogenic (glacial acetic acid — for weak bases), amphiprotic. Acetic anhydride removes water; mercuric acetate for halide salts; levelling vs differentiating.
- Mohr neutral pH 6.5–9; Volhard back titration in HNO3; modified Volhard filter or nitrobenzene (AgCl more soluble than AgSCN); Fajans fluorescein/eosin.
- Gravimetry: precipitate, digest, filter, wash, ignite, weigh. Ba = BaSO4 × 0.5884; SO4 = × 0.4116. Co-/post-precipitation.
- EDTA hexadentate, 1:1, buffered. Direct, back (Al), replacement (Ca with Mg), indirect. Masking: KCN, triethanolamine, fluoride; demasking: formaldehyde.
- Redox: oxidation = loss of e⁻. KMnO4 n = 5, H2SO4 only, autocatalysis. Ce(IV) stable, n = 1. Iodimetry direct (blue appears), iodometry indirect (blue disappears).

## Unit 4: GI agents, antimicrobials, radiopharmaceuticals

- Acidifiers: dilute HCl (achlorhydria, via straw); NaH2PO4.
- Ideal antacid: non-systemic, no CO2, no rebound, no bowel effect, prolonged. Al constipates + Mg loosens; simethicone.
- NaHCO3: Solvay (NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O); systemic; alkalosis, CO2, Na load.
- Al(OH)3 gel: alum + Na2CO3; EDTA back titration with ZnSO4, 0.002549 g Al2O3; ANC.
- Laxatives (osmotic): Mg(OH)2 (milk of magnesia), Na2HPO4, Rochelle salt, Mg trisilicate (silica gel coat).
- Antimicrobial mechanisms: oxidation, halogenation, protein precipitation.
- KMnO4 (MnO2 + KOH + KClO3 → K2MnO4 → KMnO4); boric acid (borax + acid; assay with glycerin); H2O2 (BaO2 + H2SO4; anthraquinone; 3% ≈ 10 vol; catalase foams); chlorinated lime (Cl2 + Ca(OH)2; ≥ 30% available Cl; KI + acetic acid + thio); iodine (Lugol's 5% I2 + 10% KI; povidone-iodine).
- α (paper), β (perspex), γ (lead). t½ = 0.693/λ; 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq.
- I-131 8 d thyroid; Tc-99m 6 h, 140 keV, Mo-99 generator, imaging; Co-60 5.3 y teletherapy + sterilisation; P-32 14 d polycythaemia vera.
- Time, distance, shielding (ALARA); shielded labelled storage; decay-in-storage ~10 half-lives; AERB, Atomic Energy Act 1962.

## Unit 5: Miscellaneous

- Expectorants: sedative/reflex (NH4Cl) and stimulant/direct (KI).
- KI: I2 + KOH → KI + KIO3, charcoal; Andrews assay; iodism.
- NH4Cl: NH3 + HCl; sublimes; formol assay; expectorant, systemic/urinary acidifier; avoid in liver failure.
- Emetics: central (apomorphine) vs reflex (CuSO4); never in corrosives, kerosene, unconscious. Tartar emetic = antimony potassium tartrate.
- CuSO4: Cu + conc H2SO4; KI + acetic acid, thio, KSCN near end.
- Iron absorbed as Fe²⁺ in duodenum; vitamin C ↑, antacids/tea/tetracycline ↓. FeSO4 (Fe + dil H2SO4, ~20% Fe, cerimetry, ferroin); ferrous gluconate (Ca gluconate + FeSO4, ~11.6% Fe, less irritant).
- Antidotes: physical (activated charcoal), chemical (thiosulphate, EDTA, BAL, desferrioxamine), physiological (atropine, naloxone).
- Na2S2O3: Na2SO3 + S; iodimetry; cyanide: nitrite → methaemoglobin; thiosulphate + rhodanese → thiocyanate.

questions.answer:
1. Limit test: a semi-quantitative test showing whether a known impurity is above or below a fixed limit, by comparing test and standard treated identically.
2. Principle: arsenic is converted to arsine (AsH3) by nascent hydrogen from arsenic-free zinc and HCl; arsine gives a yellow (turning brownish) stain on mercuric chloride paper; stain compared with that from standard arsenic solution.
3. Reactions: As(V) → As(III) by KI and SnCl2; Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + 2[H]; As(III) + nascent H → AsH3.
4. Reagents and roles: stannated HCl (acid, even gas evolution), KI and SnCl2 (reduce arsenate to arsenite), arsenic-free zinc (nascent H), lead acetate cotton wool (absorbs H2S), HgCl2 paper (stain).
5. Apparatus: wide-mouth bottle with rubber bung, narrow tube packed with lead acetate cotton, top end with HgCl2 paper clamped between two flat-ended tubes (draw diagram).
6. Procedure: sample dissolved, reagents added, zinc added, bung fitted, kept at about 40 °C for about 40 minutes; standard run side by side.
7. Observation: stain of test not more intense than standard → passes.
8. Precautions: arsenic-free reagents, steady temperature, compare at once (stain fades in light).
questions.question: Define limit test. Explain the principle, reagents and procedure of the limit test for arsenic, with a labelled diagram of the Gutzeit apparatus.

questions.answer:
1. Impurity: any component of a drug substance or product that is not the intended chemical entity or an excipient.
2. Types: organic (starting materials, intermediates, by-products, degradation products), inorganic (reagents, catalysts, heavy metals, chloride, sulphate), residual solvents, toxic elemental impurities (As, Pb, Hg), physical (dust, fibres, glass).
3. Sources — raw materials: rock salt carries Ca and Mg salts; sulphuric acid from pyrites carries arsenic.
4. Method of manufacture: reagents left (ammonia, chloride in NaHCO3 by Solvay process), intermediates, side reactions, solvents (water brings Ca, Mg, Cl⁻, SO4²⁻), catalysts.
5. Plant and vessels: Fe, Cu, Pb, Zn from metal vessels; alkali from glass; fibres from filters.
6. Atmosphere: dust, CO2 (NaOH → Na2CO3), moisture, SO2.
7. Storage: decomposition by light, heat, air; reaction with container; efflorescence/deliquescence; microbial contamination.
8. Cross-contamination, labelling errors, deliberate adulteration.
9. Regulatory importance: toxicity, reduced potency, shorter shelf life, changes in colour/taste; pharmacopoeia sets limits and test methods; ICH thresholds for reporting, identification and qualification; failing batches cannot be sold.
questions.question: What are impurities in pharmaceuticals? Discuss the types and sources of impurities and the regulatory importance of controlling them.

questions.answer:
1. Error = measured value − true value.
2. Determinate (systematic): definite cause, same direction, can be corrected — instrumental (uncalibrated glassware, weights), method (incomplete reaction, end point ≠ equivalence point, solubility of precipitate), reagent (impurities), personal (parallax, colour judgement). Constant or proportional. Affect accuracy.
3. Indeterminate (random): no single cause, scatter both sides of the mean; affect precision; handled by repeats and statistics.
4. Gross errors: blunders; result discarded.
5. Minimising: calibration, blank determination, control determination with a standard, independent method, parallel (replicate) determinations, standard addition, good technique.
6. Accuracy: closeness to true value (absolute or relative error).
7. Precision: closeness of repeated results (SD, RSD).
8. Example: titres 10.12, 10.15, 10.10, 10.14, 10.13 ml; mean 10.128 ml, SD 0.019, RSD 0.19% (precise); true 10.00 ml → relative error +1.28% (not accurate; systematic error suspected).
9. Precise results can still be inaccurate.
questions.question: Explain the different types of errors in pharmaceutical analysis. How are errors minimised? Define accuracy and precision with an example.

questions.answer:
1. Primary standard: pure enough to weigh directly for a solution of exactly known strength — KHP, anhydrous Na2CO3, NaCl, K2Cr2O7, KIO3, As2O3.
2. Secondary standard: strength found by titration against a primary standard — NaOH, HCl, KMnO4, Na2S2O3, iodine, AgNO3, EDTA.
3. Ideal properties: high purity (~99.9%), stable in air (not hygroscopic or efflorescent, not attacked by CO2/O2), unchanged on drying, high equivalent weight, soluble, reacts quickly and stoichiometrically, cheap and available.
questions.question: Distinguish between primary and secondary standards with two examples each. List the properties of an ideal primary standard.

questions.answer:
1. Principle: iron (Fe²⁺ or Fe³⁺) reacts with thioglycollic acid in ammoniacal solution containing citric acid to give a pink to reddish-purple ferrous thioglycollate complex; colour compared with standard iron solution.
2. Citric acid (20% w/v): complexes iron and prevents precipitation as hydroxide in alkali.
3. Thioglycollic acid: reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ and forms the coloured complex, so total iron is detected.
4. Iron-free ammonia: makes the solution alkaline; colour develops only in alkaline medium.
5. Compare after 5 minutes, viewing down Nessler cylinders against white background.
questions.question: Explain the principle of the limit test for iron and the role of each reagent.

questions.answer:
1. Chloride: Cl⁻ + AgNO3 → AgCl white opalescence in dilute HNO3; HNO3 removes interference of carbonate/phosphate and gives even opalescence; compare with standard NaCl, black background.
2. Sulphate: SO4²⁻ + BaCl2 → BaSO4 white turbidity in dilute HCl; barium sulphate reagent contains a little K2SO4 (seeding) and alcohol (prevents supersaturation); compare with standard K2SO4.
3. Modified tests: substances that interfere — effervescing carbonates (sodium bicarbonate: extra acid, wait/boil till effervescence stops), coloured substances (KMnO4: reduce with alcohol, filter MnO2, test filtrate), insoluble substances (extract prepared).
4. Standard receives the same extra reagents.
questions.question: Describe the limit tests for chloride and sulphate. Why are modified limit tests needed? Give one example.

questions.answer:
1. Heavy metals: metals giving coloured sulphides (Pb, Cu, Hg, Bi, Sb, Sn, Cd, Ag); result expressed as ppm of lead.
2. Principle: at pH about 3.5 (acetate buffer) thioacetamide releases H2S, which forms brown-black metal sulphides: M²⁺ + H2S → MS + 2H⁺.
3. Compared with standard lead solution treated identically, viewing down against white background.
4. pH 3.5 lets heavy metals precipitate while Fe and Zn interfere little.
5. Thioacetamide replaces H2S gas: safer, releases H2S evenly; different IP methods for soluble, coloured or ignited samples.
questions.question: Describe the limit test for heavy metals.

questions.answer:
1. Molarity: moles per litre of solution. Normality: gram equivalents per litre; N = M × n. Molality: moles per kg solvent. % w/w, % w/v, % v/v. ppm (µg/g). Equivalence (g of substance per ml of titrant).
2. Equivalent weight = molar mass ÷ n (H⁺, OH⁻ or electrons per formula unit).
3. Example: 4.9 g H2SO4 (98.07) in 500 ml → 0.0500 mol/0.5 L = 0.100 M = 0.200 N.

3. Preparation: NH3 + HCl → NH4Cl; or (NH4)2SO4 + 2NaCl → 2NH4Cl (sublimes) + Na2SO4.
4. Properties: white crystals, cooling saline taste, soluble, sublimes, solution slightly acid.
5. Assay (formol): sample + neutralised formaldehyde; 4NH4Cl + 6HCHO → (CH2)6N4 + 4HCl + 6H2O; titrate 0.1 M NaOH, phenolphthalein; 1 ml ≡ 0.005349 g.
6. Example: 0.1000 g, 18.65 ml, f 1.002 → 100.0%.
7. Uses: expectorant, systemic acidifier (2NH4Cl + CO2 → urea + 2HCl + H2O), urinary acidifier, mild diuretic.
8. Contraindicated in liver and kidney failure.
questions.question: What are expectorants? Classify them. Describe the preparation, properties, assay and uses of ammonium chloride.

questions.answer:
1. Haematinic: increases haemoglobin; treats anaemia; iron salts, B12, folic acid.
2. Iron absorbed as Fe²⁺ in duodenum/upper jejunum; ↑ by acid, vitamin C, deficiency; ↓ by antacids, phosphates, tea, tetracyclines; stored as ferritin.
3. Preparation: Fe + dilute H2SO4 → FeSO4 + H2; excess iron and slight acidity keep Fe²⁺; crystallise; dried form by controlled heating.
4. Properties: pale bluish-green crystals, efflorescent, oxidise in moist air to basic ferric sulphate; ~20% Fe.
5. Assay (cerimetry): ~0.5 g in dilute H2SO4 + boiled cooled water, ferroin, 0.1 M ceric ammonium sulphate; Fe²⁺ + Ce⁴⁺ → Fe³⁺ + Ce³⁺; 1 ml ≡ 0.02780 g FeSO4·7H2O; example 17.90 ml, f 1.002 → 99.7%.
6. Uses: iron-deficiency anaemia; side effects GI upset, constipation, black stools; child-proof storage.
7. Ferrous gluconate: Ca gluconate + FeSO4 → Fe gluconate + CaSO4; ~11.6% Fe; less irritant; cerimetric assay 1 ml ≡ 0.04822 g.
questions.question: What are haematinics? Discuss iron absorption. Describe the preparation, properties, assay and uses of ferrous sulphate and compare it with ferrous gluconate.

questions.answer:
1. Poison: substance that damages health or causes death by chemical action in sufficient amount. Antidote: counteracts a poison.
2. Physical/mechanical: activated charcoal (adsorbs), demulcents, gastric lavage.
3. Chemical: sodium thiosulphate (cyanide → thiocyanate), chelators (CaNa2EDTA for lead, BAL for As/Hg, desferrioxamine for iron, penicillamine for copper).
4. Physiological: atropine (organophosphates), naloxone (opioids), oxygen (CO), N-acetylcysteine (paracetamol).
5. Preparation: Na2SO3 + S (boil) → Na2S2O3; crystallise pentahydrate.
6. Properties: colourless crystals, very soluble, acids give S + SO2; reducing agent.
7. Assay (iodimetry): 0.05 M I2, starch; 2Na2S2O3 + I2 → Na2S4O6 + 2NaI; 1 ml ≡ 0.02482 g; example 20.10 ml for 0.5000 g → 99.8%.
8. Cyanide: sodium nitrite forms methaemoglobin binding CN⁻; thiosulphate is sulphur donor for rhodanese: CN⁻ + S2O3²⁻ → SCN⁻ + SO3²⁻, excreted in urine.
questions.question: Define poison and antidote. Classify antidotes with examples. Describe the preparation, assay and antidotal use of sodium thiosulphate.

questions.answer:
1. 3I2 + 6KOH → 5KI + KIO3 + 3H2O; evaporate; heat with charcoal: KIO3 + 3C → KI + 3CO; extract and crystallise.
2. Colourless crystals, very soluble, turns yellow in moist air/light.
3. Assay (Andrews): HCl, chloroform, 0.05 M KIO3 until violet colour of chloroform layer disappears; KIO3 + 2KI + 6HCl → 3ICl + 3KCl + 3H2O; 1 ml ≡ 0.01660 g.
4. Uses: expectorant, Lugol's solution, solubilises iodine, iodine source, thyroid blocking.
5. Iodism with prolonged use.
questions.question: Describe the preparation, assay and uses of potassium iodide.

questions.answer:
1. Emetic: causes vomiting; now rarely used.
2. Central (apomorphine, CTZ), reflex/local (CuSO4, ZnSO4, salt, mustard), mixed (ipecacuanha).
3. Contraindicated: corrosives, kerosene, unconscious, convulsions.
4. CuSO4: Cu + 2H2SO4 → CuSO4 + SO2 + 2H2O, or CuO + H2SO4; blue crystals, white when anhydrous.
5. Assay (iodometry): acetic acid + KI; 2Cu²⁺ + 4I⁻ → 2CuI + I2; thiosulphate, starch, KSCN near end; 1 ml 0.1 M ≡ 0.02497 g CuSO4·5H2O.
6. Other uses: astringent, fungicide (Bordeaux), Fehling's/Benedict's reagent.
questions.question: What are emetics? Classify them and describe the preparation and assay of copper sulphate.

questions.answer:
1. Cyanide binds cytochrome oxidase (Fe³⁺), blocking cell respiration.
2. Sodium nitrite oxidises part of haemoglobin to methaemoglobin (Fe³⁺), which attracts cyanide as cyanmethaemoglobin, freeing cytochrome oxidase.
3. Sodium thiosulphate donates sulphur to the enzyme rhodanese: CN⁻ + S2O3²⁻ → SCN⁻ + SO3²⁻.
4. Thiocyanate is much less toxic and excreted in urine.
5. Hydroxocobalamin is an alternative that binds cyanide directly.
questions.question: Explain the mechanism of sodium thiosulphate and sodium nitrite in cyanide poisoning.

questions.answer:
1. Iron content: FeSO4·7H2O ~20%; ferrous gluconate ~11.6%.
2. Gastric irritation: more with sulphate, less with gluconate.
3. Appearance: bluish-green crystals vs yellowish-grey/greenish-yellow powder.
4. Preparation: Fe + dilute H2SO4 vs calcium gluconate + FeSO4 (CaSO4 removed).
5. Assay: both cerimetry with ferroin; 1 ml 0.1 M Ce(IV) ≡ 0.02780 g vs 0.04822 g.
6. Both oxidise in moist air; store well closed.
questions.question: Compare ferrous sulphate and ferrous gluconate as haematinics.

questions.answer:
1. Physical/mechanical: prevent absorption — activated charcoal, demulcents (milk, egg white), gastric lavage.
2. Chemical: react with poison — sodium thiosulphate (cyanide), CaNa2EDTA (lead), dimercaprol (As, Hg), desferrioxamine (iron), penicillamine (copper).
3. Physiological/pharmacological: opposite effect or receptor block — atropine (organophosphates), naloxone (opioids), flumazenil (benzodiazepines), oxygen (CO), N-acetylcysteine (paracetamol).
4. Universal antidote (charcoal, MgO, tannic acid) is historical; activated charcoal alone is used.
questions.question: Classify antidotes with suitable examples.

questions.answer:
1. Rochelle salt, KNaC4H4O6·4H2O.
2. Preparation: cream of tartar neutralised with Na2CO3: 2KHC4H4O6 + Na2CO3 → 2KNaC4H4O6 + H2O + CO2.
3. Colourless crystals, cooling saline taste, freely soluble.
4. Uses: saline laxative, effervescent (Seidlitz-type) powders, Fehling's solution.
5. Listed under emetics in the syllabus; the classical tartrate emetic is antimony potassium tartrate (tartar emetic), now obsolete.
questions.question: Write a note on sodium potassium tartrate.

questions.answer: Boiling removes dissolved oxygen, which would oxidise Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ before titration and give a low result.
questions.question: Why is freshly boiled and cooled water used in the assay of ferrous sulphate?

# Unit 1: Introduction to pharmaceutical analysis, errors, impurities and limit tests

Every medicine has to be checked before it reaches a patient: is it the right substance, does it contain the right amount, and is it free from harmful impurities? Pharmaceutical analysis answers these three questions. This unit lays the foundation for the whole subject: the kinds of analysis, how the strength of a solution is written, standard solutions, the errors that creep into every measurement, and how the Indian Pharmacopoeia (IP) keeps impurities under control with limit tests.

## 1.1 Pharmaceutical analysis and its techniques

**Pharmaceutical analysis** is the branch of chemistry that identifies a drug (qualitative analysis), measures how much of it is present (quantitative analysis) and checks its purity, in raw materials, intermediates and finished dosage forms.

| Type | Question it answers | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Qualitative | What is present? | Identification tests of the IP (flame test for sodium, silver nitrate test for chloride) |
| Quantitative | How much is present? | Assay of sodium chloride by titration with silver nitrate |
| Limit tests / purity tests | Is an impurity below the permitted level? | Limit test for iron, arsenic, heavy metals |

**Different techniques of analysis**

| Group | Techniques | Measured quantity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chemical (classical) | Titrimetric (volumetric) analysis; gravimetric analysis | Volume of a standard solution; mass of a pure precipitate |
| Instrumental: optical | UV–visible spectrophotometry, colorimetry, IR, fluorimetry, flame photometry, atomic absorption | Absorbed or emitted light |
| Instrumental: electrochemical | Potentiometry, conductometry, polarography | Potential, conductance, current |
| Instrumental: separation | Paper, thin-layer, column, gas and high-performance liquid chromatography | Separation and response of each component |
| Physical tests | Melting point, refractive index, optical rotation, specific gravity, viscosity | A physical constant |
| Biological | Microbiological assays, bioassays | Response of an organism or tissue |

**Titrimetric (volumetric) analysis**: a solution of exactly known strength (the **titrant**) is added from a burette to the substance until the reaction is just complete (the **equivalence point**). The point where the indicator changes colour is the **end point**; a good method keeps the end point as close as possible to the equivalence point. The amount of substance is calculated from the volume used.

Types of titration by reaction: acid–base (neutralisation), non-aqueous, precipitation, complexometric and redox. By technique: **direct** (titrant added straight to the sample), **back** (excess titrant added, the excess titrated with a second standard), and **replacement** (the sample releases an equivalent amount of another species that is titrated).

## 1.2 Methods of expressing the strength of solutions

| Expression | Definition | Formula |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Molarity (M) | Moles of solute in 1 litre of solution | M = (mass in g ÷ molar mass) ÷ volume in litres |
| Normality (N) | Gram equivalents of solute in 1 litre of solution | N = M × n (n = H⁺, OH⁻ or electrons per formula unit in that reaction) |
| Molality (m) | Moles of solute in 1 kg of solvent | Does not change with temperature |
| Mole fraction | Moles of one component ÷ total moles | No units |
| Percentage | % w/w (g per 100 g), % w/v (g per 100 ml), % v/v (ml per 100 ml) | Used for pharmacopoeial solutions |
| ppm | Parts per million; 1 ppm = 1 µg per g (or about 1 µg per ml for dilute water solutions) | Used for traces and limit tests |
| Titre / equivalence | Grams of a substance equivalent to 1 ml of the titrant | Written in IP assays as "1 ml of 0.1 M … is equivalent to … g" |

**Equivalent weight** = molar mass ÷ n. For acids n is the number of replaceable H⁺ used; for bases the number of OH⁻ (or H⁺ accepted); for oxidising and reducing agents the number of electrons gained or lost per formula unit.

| Substance | Reaction | n | Normality of a 0.1 M solution |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HCl | Neutralisation | 1 | 0.1 N |
| H2SO4 | Neutralisation (both H⁺) | 2 | 0.2 N |
| Na2CO3 | Titrated to CO2 with HCl | 2 | 0.2 N |
| KMnO4 | MnO4⁻ → Mn²⁺ in acid (5 electrons) | 5 | 0.5 N |
| Na2S2O3 | 2S2O3²⁻ → S4O6²⁻ (1 electron per ion) | 1 | 0.1 N |

The IP now writes all volumetric solutions in **molarity**, so learn to convert both ways.

**Worked examples**

1. 4.9 g of H2SO4 (molar mass 98.07) in 500 ml: moles = 4.9/98.07 = 0.0500; M = 0.0500/0.500 = **0.100 M**; N = 0.100 × 2 = **0.200 N**.
2. 2.0 g NaOH (40.00) in 250 ml: M = (2.0/40.00)/0.250 = **0.200 M** (= 0.200 N).
3. To make 1 litre of 0.1 N Na2CO3 (equivalent weight 105.99/2 = 53.00): weigh **5.300 g** (this is 0.05 M).

**Basic relation used in every titration**

At the equivalence point: M1 × V1 × (ratio) = M2 × V2, or in normality N1V1 = N2V2. In IP assays the factor **f** of the titrant (actual strength ÷ nominal strength) multiplies the burette reading:

```text
% of substance = (V × f × equivalence factor × 100) ÷ weight of sample
```

## 1.3 Primary and secondary standards

A **standard solution** is a solution of accurately known concentration. It is made either by dissolving an exactly weighed amount of a primary standard, or by finding the strength of a roughly made solution by titration against a primary standard (**standardisation**).

**Primary standard**: a substance pure enough to be weighed directly to make a solution of exactly known strength.

Properties of an ideal primary standard:

1. High purity (about 99.9% or better), easy to purify and dry.
2. Stable in air: not hygroscopic, not efflorescent, not attacked by oxygen or carbon dioxide.
3. Unchanged by drying at a suitable temperature.
4. High equivalent weight, so weighing errors are small.
5. Freely soluble in the solvent used.
6. Reacts quickly, completely and in a known (stoichiometric) ratio.
7. Easily available and inexpensive.

| Primary standard | Used to standardise |
| --- | --- |
| Potassium hydrogen phthalate (KHP) | NaOH (aqueous); perchloric acid (non-aqueous) |
| Anhydrous sodium carbonate | HCl, H2SO4 |
| Benzoic acid | Sodium/lithium methoxide (non-aqueous) |
| Sodium chloride | Silver nitrate |
| Potassium dichromate, potassium bromate, potassium iodate | Sodium thiosulphate |
| Arsenic trioxide, sodium oxalate | Ceric ammonium sulphate, potassium permanganate |
| Zinc (granulated), calcium carbonate | Disodium EDTA |

**Secondary standard**: a substance whose solution cannot be made to an exact strength by weighing, so it is standardised against a primary standard. Examples: NaOH (absorbs moisture and CO2), HCl (volatile, concentration of the concentrated acid not exact), KMnO4 (contains MnO2 and decomposes), sodium thiosulphate, iodine, silver nitrate (light-sensitive), EDTA, perchloric acid.

## 1.4 Errors in analysis

An **error** is the difference between a measured value and the true value. Every measurement has some error; the analyst's job is to know where it comes from and keep it small.

**Sources of errors**

- Instrumental: uncalibrated balance, burette, pipette or flask; faulty weights.
- Method: incomplete reaction, side reactions, solubility of a precipitate, end point not matching equivalence point, co-precipitation.
- Reagents: impure chemicals, impure water.
- Personal: wrong reading of the meniscus (parallax), colour blindness for an end point, careless transfer, calculation slips.
- Environment: temperature (glassware volume and solution volume change), humidity, light (silver salts, iodine), dust.

**Types of errors**

| Type | Nature | Examples | Effect | How detected |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Determinate (systematic)** | Have a definite cause; occur in the same direction; can be found and corrected | Instrumental, method, reagent and personal errors | Lower **accuracy** | Blank, standard reference material, different method |
| **Indeterminate (random)** | No single cause; small, scatter on both sides of the mean | Small fluctuations of reading, temperature, balance drift | Lower **precision** | Repeating measurements and statistics |
| Gross error | Large mistake | Spilling, wrong pipette, wrong weight recorded | Result discarded | Obvious outlier |

Determinate errors may be **constant** (same size whatever the sample size, e.g. indicator blank) or **proportional** (grow with sample size, e.g. an interfering impurity in the sample).

**Methods of minimising errors**

1. **Calibration** of balance, weights and volumetric glassware.
2. **Blank determination**: run the procedure without the sample and subtract the blank titre (removes reagent and indicator error).
3. **Control determination**: analyse a standard substance of known purity under the same conditions.
4. **Independent method**: check the result by a different method.
5. **Parallel determinations**: do the analysis in duplicate or triplicate and accept concordant results.
6. **Standard addition**: add a known amount of analyte and see if it is fully recovered.
7. Use good technique: read the lower meniscus at eye level, wash precipitates properly, protect light-sensitive solutions, keep temperature constant.

## 1.5 Accuracy, precision and significant figures

**Accuracy**: closeness of a result to the true value. Expressed as absolute error (measured − true) or relative error (error ÷ true × 100).

**Precision**: closeness of repeated results to one another. Expressed as standard deviation (SD) or relative standard deviation (RSD, also called coefficient of variation = SD ÷ mean × 100).

```text
      Accurate and precise     Precise, not accurate     Accurate (mean), not precise
            . . .                       . . .                  .        .
           ( ◎ )                       (   ◎ )  . .            (  ◎  )
            . .                                                  .    .
   all hits near the centre     close together but off      scattered around centre
```

Good precision does not prove good accuracy: a systematic error can give close but wrong results.

**Worked example.** Five titres for a sample: 10.12, 10.15, 10.10, 10.14, 10.13 ml; true value 10.00 ml.

- Mean = 50.64/5 = **10.128 ml**
- SD (n − 1) = **0.019 ml**; RSD = 0.019/10.128 × 100 = **0.19%** (very precise)
- Absolute error = 10.128 − 10.00 = **+0.128 ml**; relative error = **+1.28%** (a systematic error is likely)

**Significant figures** are all the certain digits of a number plus the first uncertain one.

Rules:

1. All non-zero digits count (4.25 has 3).
2. Zeros between non-zero digits count (20.05 has 4).
3. Leading zeros do not count (0.0042 has 2).
4. Trailing zeros after a decimal point count (25.00 ml has 4: it says the burette was read to 0.01 ml).
5. **Addition/subtraction**: the answer keeps as many decimal places as the number with the fewest decimal places (12.11 + 0.3 + 1.234 = 13.644 → **13.6**).
6. **Multiplication/division**: the answer keeps as many significant figures as the number with the fewest (2.50 × 3.1416 = 7.854 → **7.85**).
7. Round off only at the end; if the digit to be dropped is 5 or more, round up.

## 1.6 Impurities in pharmaceuticals

An **impurity** is any component of a drug substance or product that is not the intended chemical entity (or an excipient). Impurities may be harmless, but some are toxic (arsenic, lead), some reduce the activity or shelf life (moisture, oxidising agents), and some change the appearance, taste or smell.

**Types and contents of impurities** (the modern classification used in regulatory guidelines):

| Type | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Organic impurities | Starting materials, intermediates, by-products, degradation products |
| Inorganic impurities | Reagents, catalysts, heavy metals, inorganic salts (chloride, sulphate), filter aids |
| Residual solvents | Solvents left from manufacture |
| Toxic impurities | Arsenic, lead, mercury and other elemental impurities |
| Physical impurities | Dust, fibres, glass particles |

**Regulatory importance**

- Impurities can harm the patient directly (toxic metals), cause allergy, or lower the dose of active drug.
- They can catalyse decomposition, change colour, odour or taste, and shorten the shelf life.
- Pharmacopoeias (IP, BP, USP) fix limits for each impurity in a monograph and give the method of testing; a batch that fails cannot be sold.
- International guidelines (ICH) set thresholds for reporting, identifying and qualifying impurities and limits for residual solvents and elemental impurities.
- Limit tests and impurity profiles are part of quality control and of the documents submitted for approval of a drug.

## 1.7 Sources of impurities

```text
  Raw materials ─┐
  Method of      │
  manufacture ───┤
  Reagents and   ├──►  IMPURITY IN THE FINAL PRODUCT
  solvents ──────┤
  Plant/vessels ─┤
  Storage and ───┤
  decomposition  │
  Adulteration ──┘
```

1. **Raw materials**: natural minerals carry other elements. Rock salt contains calcium and magnesium salts; sulphuric acid made from pyrites may carry arsenic.
2. **Method of manufacture**:
   - Reagents left behind (sodium carbonate in sodium bicarbonate made by the Solvay process may contain ammonia and chloride).
   - Intermediate products or incomplete reaction.
   - Side reactions and by-products.
   - Solvents (water itself brings calcium, magnesium, chloride, sulphate; organic solvents may remain).
   - Catalysts (nickel, platinum).
3. **Reaction vessels and plant**: iron, copper, lead or zinc dissolve from metal vessels and pipes; glass gives alkali; filter aids give fibres.
4. **Atmospheric contamination**: dust, sulphur dioxide, carbon dioxide (NaOH absorbs CO2 and forms sodium carbonate), moisture.
5. **Storage**: chemical decomposition (light, heat, air), reaction with the container, contamination by insects or microbes, loss of water of crystallisation (efflorescence) or absorption of moisture (deliquescence), physical changes in crystal form.
6. **Manufacturing hazards**: cross-contamination from other products in the same plant, particles from machines, mistakes in labelling.
7. **Deliberate adulteration**: cheaper material added for profit.

## 1.8 Limit tests: the general idea

A **limit test** is a semi-quantitative test that shows whether a known impurity is present in an amount **above or below a fixed limit**. The sample (test) and a **standard** with exactly the permitted amount of impurity are treated identically, side by side, and the turbidity, opalescence, colour or stain is compared.

General rules:

- Use a matched pair of **Nessler cylinders** (same glass, size and diameter).
- Add the same reagents in the same order and volume to test and standard.
- Compare after the same time, viewing **down the length of the cylinder** against a black background (turbidity) or a white background (colour).
- If the test is less turbid or less coloured than the standard, the sample **passes**.

Why a limit test instead of a full assay? The impurity is present in traces; an exact value is not needed, only proof that it is below a safe limit; the test is quick and cheap.

## 1.9 Limit test for chloride

**Principle.** Chloride reacts with silver nitrate in the presence of dilute nitric acid to give a white opalescence of silver chloride.

Cl⁻ + AgNO3 → AgCl (white opalescence) + NO3⁻

**Role of dilute nitric acid**: dissolves carbonates, phosphates and other anions (which would also precipitate silver) and makes the opalescence fine and even.

**Procedure (outline).** Dissolve the stated amount of sample in water in a Nessler cylinder, add dilute nitric acid, make up to volume, add silver nitrate solution, stir and stand for about 5 minutes protected from light. Prepare a standard with a known volume of standard sodium chloride solution in the same way. Compare the opalescence against a black background. The older IP standard used 1 ml of 0.05845% w/v sodium chloride solution; follow the current IP for the exact quantity.

## 1.10 Limit test for sulphate

**Principle.** Sulphate reacts with barium chloride in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid to give a white turbidity of barium sulphate.

SO4²⁻ + BaCl2 → BaSO4 (white turbidity) + 2Cl⁻

**Reagents.** Barium sulphate reagent (barium chloride with a little potassium sulphate in alcohol). The small amount of potassium sulphate **seeds** the precipitation, so the turbidity forms quickly and evenly; alcohol prevents supersaturation and keeps particles fine. Hydrochloric acid prevents the precipitation of other barium salts (carbonate, phosphate).

**Standard.** A known volume of standard potassium sulphate solution (the older IP used 0.1089% w/v K2SO4), treated the same way. Compare turbidity after about 5 minutes.

## 1.11 Modified limit tests for chloride and sulphate

Some substances cannot be tested by the general method because they interfere with it. The test is **modified** to remove the interference, and the standard receives the same extra reagents.

| Problem | Example | Modification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Substance is a carbonate or bicarbonate (effervesces with acid; CO2 disturbs the test) | Sodium bicarbonate, sodium carbonate | Extra acid added; solution allowed to stand or boiled until effervescence stops |
| Substance is strongly coloured | Potassium permanganate | Colour destroyed first (reduced with alcohol and warmed); brown MnO2 filtered; clear filtrate tested |
| Substance is insoluble in water | Some insoluble salts and oxides | An acid solution or a water extract is prepared and filtered, then tested |
| Substance itself reacts with the reagent | Salts precipitated by silver or barium | Interfering ion removed or converted first |

Examiners usually want the **reason** for modification and one example with the exact change made.

## 1.12 Limit test for iron

**Principle.** Iron, as Fe³⁺ or Fe²⁺, reacts with **thioglycollic acid** in a solution made alkaline with ammonia in the presence of **citric acid**, giving a pale pink to deep reddish-purple colour (ferrous thioglycollate complex).

| Reagent | Role |
| --- | --- |
| Citric acid (20% w/v) | Forms a soluble complex with iron and stops it precipitating as hydroxide when ammonia is added |
| Thioglycollic acid | Reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ and forms the coloured complex, so all iron is detected whatever its state |
| Iron-free ammonia | Makes the solution alkaline; the colour develops only in alkaline medium |

The standard uses standard iron solution (from ferric ammonium sulphate). The colours are compared after about 5 minutes, viewing down against a white background.

## 1.13 Limit test for arsenic (Gutzeit test)

Arsenic is highly toxic and accumulates in the body, so its limit is very low (a few ppm).

**Principle.** Arsenic in the sample is converted to **arsine gas (AsH3)** by nascent hydrogen produced from arsenic-free zinc and hydrochloric acid. Arsine passes up the tube and gives a **yellow stain** (turning brownish) on **mercuric chloride paper**. The length and intensity of the stain are compared with that from a standard arsenic solution.

```text
  As(V) ──KI, SnCl2──► As(III) ──Zn + HCl (nascent H)──► AsH3 ↑ ──HgCl2 paper──► yellow stain

        GUTZEIT APPARATUS
        ┌──────────────┐  ← HgCl2 paper held between two flat-ended glass tubes (clamped)
        │      ▲       │
        │ lead acetate │  ← cotton wool soaked in lead acetate (traps H2S)
        │  cotton wool │
        └──────┬───────┘
               │ narrow tube
        ┌──────┴───────┐
        │  wide-mouth  │  ← sample + stannated HCl + KI + SnCl2 + zinc
        │    bottle    │
        └──────────────┘
```

| Reagent | Role |
| --- | --- |
| Arsenic-free zinc | With HCl gives nascent hydrogen |
| Stannated hydrochloric acid | Acid medium; stannous chloride gives even evolution of gas |
| Potassium iodide | Reduces pentavalent arsenic (arsenate) to trivalent (arsenite), which forms arsine faster |
| Stannous chloride | Also reduces As(V) to As(III) and helps steady gas evolution |
| Lead acetate cotton wool | Absorbs hydrogen sulphide (from sulphide impurity) which would also stain the paper |
| Mercuric chloride paper | Gives the yellow-brown stain with arsine |

Precautions: all reagents arsenic-free; reaction at about 40 °C for a steady stream; test and standard run together; read the stain at once because it fades in light.

## 1.14 Limit test for lead

**Principle.** Lead forms a **red complex (lead dithizonate)** with **dithizone** (diphenylthiocarbazone) in alkaline solution. Dithizone itself is green in chloroform; the red lead complex is extracted into chloroform and its colour compared with a standard lead solution.

| Reagent | Role |
| --- | --- |
| Ammonium citrate | Keeps metals in solution in the alkaline medium |
| Potassium cyanide | Forms stable complexes with other metals (copper, zinc, nickel), which then do not react with dithizone |
| Hydroxylamine hydrochloride | Reduces Fe³⁺, which would otherwise oxidise dithizone |
| Dithizone in chloroform | Forms the red lead complex that moves into the chloroform layer |

Potassium cyanide is very poisonous: it is handled with care and never pipetted by mouth.

## 1.15 Limit test for heavy metals

"Heavy metals" means metals that form coloured sulphides under the test conditions (lead, copper, mercury, bismuth, antimony, tin, cadmium, silver). The result is expressed **as lead, in ppm**.

**Principle.** In a solution buffered at **pH about 3.5** with acetate buffer, **thioacetamide** releases hydrogen sulphide, which converts heavy metals to dark brown or black sulphides. The colour is compared with a standard made from standard lead solution.

M²⁺ + H2S → MS (brown/black) + 2H⁺

At pH 3.5 most heavy metals precipitate as sulphides, while iron, zinc and similar metals interfere little. Thioacetamide has replaced hydrogen sulphide gas because it is safer and gives H2S slowly and evenly. The IP gives different methods (A, B and others) depending on whether the substance dissolves in water, gives a coloured solution, or must first be ignited.

## 1.16 Summary of limit tests

| Test | Key reagent | Medium | Product seen | Compared as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Chloride | Silver nitrate | Dilute HNO3 | White opalescence (AgCl) | Turbidity, black background |
| Sulphate | Barium sulphate reagent | Dilute HCl | White turbidity (BaSO4) | Turbidity, black background |
| Iron | Thioglycollic acid + citric acid | Ammonia (alkaline) | Pink-purple colour | Colour, white background |
| Arsenic | Zn + HCl, KI, SnCl2 | Acid | Yellow-brown stain on HgCl2 paper | Stain |
| Lead | Dithizone in chloroform | Alkaline, citrate, cyanide | Red colour in chloroform | Colour |
| Heavy metals | Thioacetamide | Acetate buffer pH 3.5 | Brown-black sulphides | Colour, white background |

## Remember

- Analysis = identity (qualitative), amount (quantitative, assay) and purity (limit tests).
- N = M × n; H2SO4 0.1 M = 0.2 N; KMnO4 0.02 M = 0.1 N in acid.
- Primary standards: KHP, anhydrous Na2CO3, NaCl, K2Cr2O7, KIO3, As2O3, zinc. Secondary: NaOH, HCl, KMnO4, thiosulphate, iodine, AgNO3, EDTA.
- Determinate errors affect accuracy and can be corrected (blank, calibration, control); random errors affect precision and are handled by repeats and statistics.
- Accuracy = closeness to true value; precision = closeness of repeats.
- Sources of impurities: raw materials, manufacturing process, plant, atmosphere, storage, cross-contamination, adulteration.
- Limit test pairs: Cl⁻/AgNO3/HNO3; SO4²⁻/BaCl2/HCl; Fe/thioglycollic acid; As/Gutzeit/HgCl2 paper; Pb/dithizone; heavy metals/thioacetamide pH 3.5.
- Modified limit tests remove an interference (effervescence, colour, insolubility) and treat the standard the same way.

# Unit 2: Acid–base chemistry, buffers, isotonicity and electrolytes

Most drugs are weak acids or weak bases, and the body itself keeps its pH and salt balance within narrow limits. This unit explains what acids, bases and buffers are, how to calculate the pH of a buffer, why eye drops and injections must be isotonic, and which electrolytes are used to replace what the body loses.

## 2.1 Definitions of acids and bases

| Theory | Acid | Base | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Arrhenius | Gives H⁺ ions in water | Gives OH⁻ ions in water | HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻; NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻ |
| Brønsted–Lowry | Proton (H⁺) donor | Proton acceptor | NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4⁺ + OH⁻ (water is the acid here) |
| Lewis | Electron-pair acceptor | Electron-pair donor | BF3 (acid) + NH3 (base) → F3B–NH3 |

**Conjugate pairs (Brønsted–Lowry).** When an acid gives up a proton, what remains is its conjugate base: CH3COOH ⇌ CH3COO⁻ + H⁺. A strong acid has a weak conjugate base and vice versa.

**Amphiprotic substances** can act as both acid and base: water, bicarbonate (HCO3⁻), amino acids.

**Strong and weak.** A strong acid (HCl, HNO3, H2SO4, HClO4) or strong base (NaOH, KOH) ionises completely in water. A weak acid (acetic acid, boric acid, carbonic acid) or weak base (ammonia, most alkaloids) ionises only partly; its strength is given by the dissociation constant Ka or Kb, usually written as pKa = −log Ka.

HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ Ka = [H⁺][A⁻] ÷ [HA]

The lower the pKa, the stronger the acid. Acetic acid pKa about 4.76; boric acid about 9.2; ammonium ion about 9.25 (so ammonia pKb about 4.75).

## 2.2 The pH scale and its significance

Water ionises slightly: H2O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻, Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.

**pH** = −log[H⁺]; **pOH** = −log[OH⁻]; pH + pOH = 14 (at 25 °C).

```text
 0 ────────── 3 ────────── 7 ─────────── 11 ────────── 14
 strongly acid    weakly acid   neutral   weakly alkaline  strongly alkaline
 (gastric juice ~1–2)          (pure water)   (blood 7.35–7.45)
```

A change of 1 pH unit means a tenfold change in [H⁺].

**Quick calculations**

- 0.1 M HCl (strong): [H⁺] = 0.1 → pH = **1**.
- 0.1 M acetic acid (pKa 4.76): [H⁺] = √(Ka × C) = √(1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.1) → pH = ½(pKa − log C) = ½(4.76 + 1) = **2.88**.
- 0.1 M ammonia (pKb 4.75): pOH = ½(4.75 + 1) = 2.875 → pH = **11.12**.

**Significance of pH in pharmacy**

| Area | Why pH matters |
| --- | --- |
| Stability | Many drugs hydrolyse or oxidise faster at certain pH (esters, penicillins, adrenaline); formulations are buffered at the pH of best stability |
| Solubility | Weak acids dissolve better in alkaline, weak bases in acid solution; wrong pH causes precipitation |
| Absorption | Only the un-ionised form crosses membranes easily (pH-partition theory) |
| Comfort | Eye drops and injections far from body pH cause pain and irritation |
| Activity | Preservatives such as benzoic acid act only in the un-ionised (acid) form |
| Body | Blood pH 7.35–7.45; below 7.35 is acidosis, above 7.45 alkalosis |
| Analysis | Titrations, complexometry and limit tests need set pH ranges |

## 2.3 Buffers

A **buffer** is a solution that resists a change in pH when small amounts of acid or alkali are added, or when it is diluted.

**Types**

1. **Acidic buffer**: a weak acid + its salt with a strong base (acetic acid + sodium acetate; boric acid + borax).
2. **Basic buffer**: a weak base + its salt with a strong acid (ammonia + ammonium chloride).
3. Salt of a polybasic acid in two forms (NaH2PO4 + Na2HPO4, the phosphate buffer).

**How a buffer works (acetate buffer)**

```text
 Add acid (H⁺):    CH3COO⁻ + H⁺   → CH3COOH      (H⁺ removed by the salt)
 Add alkali (OH⁻): CH3COOH + OH⁻  → CH3COO⁻ + H2O (OH⁻ removed by the acid)
```

So the added H⁺ or OH⁻ is converted into the weak partner, and only the ratio salt : acid changes slightly.

**Pharmaceutical buffers and uses**

| Buffer | Approximate useful range | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acetate | pH 3.8–5.8 | Parenteral and oral solutions, analysis |
| Phosphate | pH 6–8 | Injections, ophthalmic solutions, dissolution media |
| Borate (boric acid/borax) | pH 7–9 | Eye drops (not for injections) |
| Citrate | pH 3–6 | Syrups, injections |
| Ammonia/ammonium chloride | about pH 10 | Complexometric titrations |

**Ideal buffer for a formulation:** adequate capacity at the required pH, non-toxic, compatible with the drug, stable, does not support microbial growth, and (for eye and injection use) does not irritate.

**Buffer capacity (β)** is the amount of strong acid or base (in gram equivalents per litre) needed to change the pH by one unit: β = ΔB ÷ ΔpH. Capacity is highest when salt = acid (pH = pKa) and when the total concentration is high. A buffer works best within about pKa ± 1.

**Physiological buffers**: bicarbonate/carbonic acid (main buffer of plasma), phosphate (inside cells and in urine), proteins including haemoglobin.

## 2.4 Buffer equation and calculation of pH

The **Henderson–Hasselbalch equation** comes from the Ka expression of a weak acid:

```text
 Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]   →   [H⁺] = Ka [HA]/[A⁻]   →   take −log:

 Acidic buffer:  pH = pKa + log ([salt] / [acid])
 Basic buffer:   pOH = pKb + log ([salt] / [base]),  pH = 14 − pOH
```

Assumptions: the acid and salt concentrations equal what was added (weak acid barely ionised, salt fully ionised); it fails for very dilute or very concentrated solutions.

**Worked examples** (acetic acid pKa 4.76)

1. 0.1 M acetic acid + 0.2 M sodium acetate: pH = 4.76 + log(0.2/0.1) = 4.76 + 0.301 = **5.06**.
2. Equal concentrations of acid and salt: log 1 = 0, so pH = pKa = **4.76**.
3. Effect of acid: 1 litre of buffer with 0.1 mol acetic acid and 0.1 mol acetate; add 0.01 mol HCl. Acetate becomes 0.09 mol, acetic acid 0.11 mol. pH = 4.76 + log(0.09/0.11) = **4.67** (a fall of only 0.09; the same HCl in 1 litre of water would give pH 2).
4. Ratio needed for pH 5.0: log(salt/acid) = 5.0 − 4.76 = 0.24 → salt : acid = **1.74 : 1**.
5. Basic buffer: 0.1 M NH3 + 0.1 M NH4Cl (pKb 4.75): pOH = 4.75 → pH = **9.25**.

## 2.5 Isotonicity

**Osmosis**: movement of water through a semipermeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated one. **Osmotic pressure** depends on the number of particles dissolved, not their nature (a colligative property).

| Term | Meaning | Effect on red blood cells |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Isotonic** | Same osmotic pressure as body fluids (0.9% w/v NaCl) | No change |
| **Hypotonic** | Lower osmotic pressure | Water enters; cells swell and burst (haemolysis) |
| **Hypertonic** | Higher osmotic pressure | Water leaves; cells shrink (crenation) |

```text
  Hypotonic        Isotonic        Hypertonic
   water in         no net          water out
    (  O  )         ( o )            (*)
   swells,         normal          shrinks,
   bursts                          crenated
```

"Iso-osmotic" refers to equal osmotic pressure measured physically; "isotonic" refers to the effect on a living membrane. Some iso-osmotic solutions (for example boric acid solutions) are not isotonic to red cells because the solute passes through the cell membrane.

Blood plasma and tears both freeze at about **−0.52 °C**. A 0.9% w/v NaCl solution has the same freezing point, so it is isotonic.

**Methods of adjusting tonicity**

1. **Freezing point depression (cryoscopic) method.** The amount of NaCl (W, g per 100 ml) needed is:

```text
 W = (0.52 − a) / b
 a = freezing point depression caused by the drug at its strength
     (= % of drug × FPD of a 1% solution)
 b = FPD of 1% w/v NaCl = 0.576 °C
```

2. **Sodium chloride equivalent (E) method.** E is the weight of NaCl giving the same osmotic effect as 1 g of the drug. NaCl to add = 0.9 g per 100 ml − (grams of drug × E).

3. **Graphical / White–Vincent method**: the drug is dissolved in enough water to make it isotonic, then made up with an isotonic vehicle.

**Worked example (made-up drug).** A 1.5% w/v eye drop of drug X; FPD of a 1% solution of X = 0.10 °C.

- a = 1.5 × 0.10 = 0.15 °C
- W = (0.52 − 0.15) ÷ 0.576 = **0.64 g NaCl per 100 ml**
- Check with E: E = 0.10/0.576 = 0.174; 1.5 g × 0.174 = 0.26 g NaCl-equivalent; NaCl needed = 0.90 − 0.26 = **0.64 g** — the same answer.

**Applications**

| Product | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| IV fluids (large volumes) | Must be isotonic or close to it; large volumes of hypotonic fluid cause haemolysis. Hypertonic solutions (concentrated dextrose for nutrition) are given slowly into a large central vein. Examples: Sodium Chloride Injection 0.9%, Dextrose 5%, Ringer's and compound sodium lactate solutions |
| Small-volume injections | Ideally isotonic, especially subcutaneous and intramuscular (less pain); intrathecal injections must be isotonic |
| Ophthalmic solutions | Should be isotonic with tears (eye tolerates about 0.6–2% NaCl equivalent); also buffered near pH 7.4 if stability allows, sterile and particle-free |
| Nasal drops, enemas, wound washes | Isotonic for comfort and to avoid damage to tissue |

## 2.6 Major extracellular and intracellular electrolytes

**Electrolytes** are substances that ionise in body water. About 60% of body weight is water: about two-thirds inside cells (intracellular fluid, ICF) and one-third outside (extracellular fluid, ECF: plasma and interstitial fluid).

| Fluid | Main cation | Main anions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Extracellular | **Sodium (Na⁺)** | **Chloride (Cl⁻)**, bicarbonate (HCO3⁻) |
| Intracellular | **Potassium (K⁺)**, magnesium (Mg²⁺) | **Phosphate**, proteins |

Usual plasma values (adult): sodium about 135–145 mEq/L; potassium about 3.5–5.0 mEq/L; chloride about 98–106 mEq/L; bicarbonate about 22–28 mEq/L; calcium about 8.5–10.5 mg/dL.

The difference between ECF and ICF is kept by the **Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump** in every cell membrane (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in).

**Units:** milliequivalent (mEq) = millimoles × valency. 1 g NaCl = 1000/58.44 = 17.1 mmol = **17.1 mEq** Na⁺; 1 g KCl = 1000/74.55 = **13.4 mEq** K⁺. 0.9% NaCl contains about 154 mmol each of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ per litre (about 308 mOsm/L).

## 2.7 Functions of major physiological ions

| Ion | Main functions | Too little / too much |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Sodium** | Main ECF cation; controls ECF volume, osmotic pressure and blood pressure; nerve impulse and muscle contraction; absorption of glucose and amino acids | Hyponatraemia: confusion, weakness; hypernatraemia: thirst, oedema |
| **Potassium** | Main ICF cation; resting membrane potential; heart rhythm; nerve and muscle function; enzyme activity | Hypokalaemia: weakness, cramps, arrhythmia; hyperkalaemia: dangerous arrhythmia |
| **Calcium** | Bones and teeth; blood clotting (factor IV); muscle contraction; nerve transmission; heart contraction; hormone release | Hypocalcaemia: tetany; hypercalcaemia: stones, weakness |
| **Chloride** | Main ECF anion with sodium; osmotic balance; gastric HCl; chloride shift in red cells | Follows sodium and acid–base changes |
| **Bicarbonate** | Main plasma buffer; carries CO2 | Low: metabolic acidosis; high: alkalosis |
| **Phosphate** | Bones and teeth, ATP, nucleic acids, phospholipids; buffer in cells and urine | — |
| **Magnesium** | Cofactor of many enzymes (ATP reactions); nerve and muscle function | Low: tremor, arrhythmia |

## 2.8 Electrolytes used in replacement therapy

Replacement therapy restores water and ions lost by vomiting, diarrhoea, burns, sweating, surgery or use of diuretics.

### Sodium chloride (NaCl, molar mass 58.44)

- **Preparation**: from sea water or brine by evaporation; purified by passing HCl gas into a saturated solution, when pure NaCl separates (common ion effect).
- **Properties**: colourless cubic crystals or white powder, salty taste, freely soluble in water.
- **Assay (IP principle)**: precipitation titration with 0.1 M silver nitrate, potassium chromate indicator (Mohr), or the modified Volhard method (see Unit 3). **1 ml of 0.1 M AgNO3 ≡ 0.005844 g NaCl** (58.44 × 0.1/1000).
- **Uses**: electrolyte replenisher (0.9% injection, oral salt), to make solutions isotonic, nasal and wound washing, hypertonic solutions for some conditions, in ORS.

### Potassium chloride (KCl, 74.55)

- Prepared from natural minerals (sylvine, carnallite) and purified by crystallisation.
- White crystals, freely soluble, saline taste.
- Assay: argentometric titration, 1 ml of 0.1 M AgNO3 ≡ 0.007455 g KCl (74.55 × 0.1/1000; derived from the 1 : 1 reaction).
- Uses: hypokalaemia (diuretic therapy, vomiting, diarrhoea), in ORS. Intravenous potassium must always be diluted and given slowly because a high plasma potassium stops the heart; never given as a rapid injection.

### Calcium chloride (CaCl2·2H2O, 147.01)

- Prepared by dissolving calcium carbonate in hydrochloric acid: CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2.
- White, hygroscopic/deliquescent fragments or granules, very soluble.
- Assay: complexometric titration with 0.05 M disodium EDTA; 1 ml of 0.05 M EDTA ≡ 0.007351 g CaCl2·2H2O (derived, 1 : 1).
- Uses: calcium replacement in hypocalcaemia and tetany; in Ringer's solution. Irritant to tissues, so given intravenously only, slowly.

### Oral Rehydration Salt (ORS)

ORS is a mixture of glucose and salts dissolved in clean water and taken by mouth to treat dehydration, mainly from diarrhoea.

**Principle**: in the small intestine, glucose and sodium are absorbed **together** by a co-transporter (SGLT1), and water follows by osmosis. This pathway keeps working even during diarrhoea such as cholera, so oral glucose–salt solution replaces losses without an injection.

**Reduced-osmolarity ORS (WHO/UNICEF, also in the IP)**, per litre of water:

| Ingredient | g per litre | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sodium chloride | 2.6 | Sodium and chloride |
| Glucose, anhydrous | 13.5 | Drives sodium (and water) absorption |
| Potassium chloride | 1.5 | Replaces potassium lost in stools |
| Trisodium citrate dihydrate | 2.9 | Corrects acidosis (citrate → bicarbonate); more stable than sodium bicarbonate |

This gives about Na⁺ 75, Cl⁻ 65, K⁺ 20, citrate 10 and glucose 75 mmol per litre; total osmolarity about **245 mOsm/L**. The lower osmolarity (compared with the older 311 mOsm/L formula) reduces stool output and vomiting. Zinc supplements are given alongside ORS in children with diarrhoea.

## 2.9 Physiological acid–base balance

Normal arterial blood pH is **7.35–7.45**. The body keeps it there by three lines of defence:

```text
  Acid/base load
      │
      ▼
 1. Buffers (seconds)      HCO3⁻/H2CO3, phosphate, proteins, haemoglobin
      │
      ▼
 2. Lungs (minutes)        CO2 blown off faster or slower by changing breathing
      │
      ▼
 3. Kidneys (hours–days)   excrete H⁺ (as NH4⁺, H2PO4⁻) and reabsorb or make HCO3⁻
```

**Bicarbonate buffer**: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H⁺ + HCO3⁻. The pH depends on the ratio [HCO3⁻] : [H2CO3], normally about **20 : 1** (pKa about 6.1; 6.1 + log 20 ≈ 7.4).

**Disturbances**

| Disorder | Primary change | Common causes | Compensation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Metabolic acidosis | HCO3⁻ falls | Diabetic ketoacidosis, kidney failure, severe diarrhoea | Fast deep breathing (loses CO2) |
| Metabolic alkalosis | HCO3⁻ rises | Prolonged vomiting, excess antacid (sodium bicarbonate) | Slow breathing |
| Respiratory acidosis | CO2 retained | Lung disease, depressed breathing | Kidneys retain HCO3⁻ |
| Respiratory alkalosis | CO2 lost | Hyperventilation (anxiety, high altitude) | Kidneys excrete HCO3⁻ |

Pharmaceutical agents: sodium bicarbonate and sodium lactate/citrate (alkalinisers, for acidosis); ammonium chloride (acidifier, for alkalosis; see Unit 5).

## Remember

- Arrhenius (H⁺/OH⁻), Brønsted–Lowry (proton donor/acceptor), Lewis (electron-pair acceptor/donor).
- pH = −log[H⁺]; pH + pOH = 14; blood 7.35–7.45.
- Buffer = weak acid + its salt (or weak base + its salt); best near pH = pKa; capacity β = ΔB/ΔpH.
- pH = pKa + log(salt/acid); pOH = pKb + log(salt/base).
- Isotonic = 0.9% NaCl = freezing point −0.52 °C; W = (0.52 − a)/0.576.
- ECF: Na⁺, Cl⁻, HCO3⁻; ICF: K⁺, Mg²⁺, phosphate.
- 1 g NaCl = 17.1 mEq Na⁺; 1 g KCl = 13.4 mEq K⁺.
- ORS per litre: NaCl 2.6 g, glucose 13.5 g, KCl 1.5 g, trisodium citrate 2.9 g; 245 mOsm/L; works by sodium–glucose co-transport.
- Bicarbonate : carbonic acid = 20 : 1 at pH 7.4; buffers → lungs → kidneys.
